# From VHDL to SystemVerilog {#sec-sv-crashcourse}

Most of you already design digital circuits in VHDL. This chapter is a crash course that maps what you know from VHDL onto synthesizable **SystemVerilog**, the hardware description language (HDL) we use throughout this course. It is not an introduction to digital design: the synchronous, latch-free design style you learned with VHDL carries over unchanged, and only the syntax and a few semantic rules are new. Along the way, you write testbenches in SystemVerilog and in Python with **cocotb**, and you lint, simulate, and synthesize your designs in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container.

::: {.callout-note}
All code of this chapter (RTL, VHDL references, testbenches, and the solutions of the exercises) is available in the folder [`content/sv_crashcourse/code`]({{< meta var.url-repo >}}/tree/main/content/sv_crashcourse/code) of the course repository, with one folder per design. The SystemVerilog code follows the layout of a macro in the AMS chip template: the RTL in `rtl/` and the testbenches in `testbenches/verilog/` and `testbenches/cocotb/`. The VHDL versions are in `vhdl/`, the plain Verilog original of the priority encoder exercise is in `verilog/`, and the lint exercise keeps its file with deliberate mistakes in `exercise/`. Every file in `rtl/` lints without warnings and synthesizes, and all testbenches pass with the tools of the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS image `2026.10`: Verilator 5.052, Icarus Verilog 14.0, cocotb 2.1.0, GHDL 7.0.0-dev (for the VHDL files), and Yosys 0.70. With another image, the cell counts in the solutions can differ slightly.
:::

## Learning Objectives {#sec-sv-objectives}

After this chapter, you will be able to:

- explain how a hardware description differs from software for a microcontroller
- describe a synchronous sequential circuit as a register plus next-state logic, and explain why the combinational logic has one clock period to compute
- name the main families of HDLs and judge their strengths and weaknesses
- translate VHDL designs written in the two-process style into idiomatic SystemVerilog
- read plain Verilog, e.g., netlists and older IP, and translate Verilog RTL into SystemVerilog
- write synthesizable combinational and sequential logic with `always_comb` and `always_ff`, and avoid latches, races, and width errors
- write self-checking testbenches in SystemVerilog and in Python with cocotb
- lint, simulate, and synthesize a design in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container by typing the commands yourself, and explain what the corresponding make targets of the AMS chip template do

## Recap: Microcontroller Software versus Hardware Description {#sec-sv-mcu-vs-hdl}

A C program for a microcontroller (MCU) and a SystemVerilog module may look alike: both have variables, operators, `if`, and `for`. Yet they describe fundamentally different things. The C program is a list of instructions that a fixed processor executes one after another. The program counter selects the next instruction, and the time a computation takes follows from the number of executed instructions. A hardware description, in contrast, describes the circuit itself. After synthesis, every line has become gates and flip-flops, and all of them work at the same time, all the time. Time is explicit: the registers update at the clock edge, and the combinational logic between them has one clock period to settle. @tbl-sv-mcu-vs-hdl summarizes the differences.

| Aspect | Software for an MCU (e.g., C) | Hardware description (HDL) |
|------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| What is described | a sequence of instructions for a fixed processor | the structure and behavior of the circuit itself |
| Execution | one instruction after another, controlled by the program counter | all statements and blocks operate concurrently, all the time |
| Time | implicit, follows from the number of instructions | explicit, every register updates at the clock edge |
| A variable is | a memory location or a CPU register | a wire (combinational logic) or a flip-flop, inferred from how it is assigned |
| A loop is | a repetition in time | a repetition in space: unrolled into parallel hardware, the bound must be a constant |
| A function call is | a jump to shared code | a separate copy of the hardware for every call |
| Compilation result | machine code in the flash memory | a netlist of gates and flip-flops, then a layout (GDSII) |
| Cost | memory and clock cycles | area, power, and maximum clock frequency |
| Debugging | debugger, `printf`, single steps on the target | simulation and waveforms before the tapeout, little visibility in silicon |
| Fixing a bug | a firmware update | for an ASIC, a new mask set and fabrication run, which takes months |

: Software for a microcontroller versus a hardware description {#tbl-sv-mcu-vs-hdl}

The most important consequence is a change in thinking: **think hardware first, then write the code.** Before you write a module, sketch its block diagram with the registers and the combinational logic between them (@sec-sv-sync-design). The code then only describes this diagram. Keep in mind that a simulator executes your HDL as an event-driven program on your computer. This is why HDLs also contain constructs such as delays, `$display`, or file access, which only make sense in simulation and cannot be synthesized (@sec-sv-synthesizable).

In the course project (@sec-project), you need both ways of thinking. You build a RISC-V SoC: the CPU and the blocks around it are hardware that you describe as registers and combinational logic, and the CPU runs firmware that you write as for any microcontroller. Many SoCs today contain such a processor core, because the firmware keeps the digital part flexible: a new feature or a bug fix in the control flow needs a firmware update instead of a new mask set, while dedicated hardware handles the time-critical parts. RISC-V is a popular choice for this core, since its instruction set is open and can be used and extended without license fees. TinyWhisper (@sec-intro-tinywhisper) is an example, with its modem in C firmware on the RISC-V CPU and its IQ modulator in dedicated hardware.

### Computing in Time and in Space {#sec-sv-time-space}

The difference between software and hardware becomes obvious with a loop. The following C function counts the ones in a byte (population count):

```c
uint8_t popcount(uint8_t x)
{
  uint8_t count = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++)
    count += (x >> i) & 1;
  return count;
}
```

In the loop body, `(x >> i) & 1` shifts bit `i` of `x` into the least significant position and clears all other bits, so `count` grows by one exactly when bit `i` is set. The same function written in SystemVerilog looks almost identical, but the hardware behind it is not a loop at all:

```{.systemverilog filename="popcount/rtl/popcount.sv"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/popcount/rtl/popcount.sv >}}
```

In the loop body, `x_i[i]` selects bit `i` directly, without a shift and a mask, and the size cast `4'(...)` (@sec-sv-operators) extends this 1-bit value explicitly to the 4 bits of `count_o`, which SystemVerilog would otherwise do silently.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: Loops in Software and in Hardware"}
1. Roughly how many clock cycles does an MCU need for the C function? How long does the hardware need?
2. What does the synthesis tool build from the `for` loop in `popcount.sv`? Is there a loop counter `i` in the hardware?
3. What changes in both cases when `x` has 64 bits instead of 8?
4. Optional, if you already have the container running: save the listing as `popcount.sv`, synthesize it with `yosys -p "read_verilog -sv popcount.sv; synth -top popcount; stat"`, and look at the cell statistics at the end of the log (@sec-sv-tools-yosys explains the command).
:::

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution: Loops in Software and in Hardware" collapse="true"}
1. Per iteration, the MCU executes a shift, an AND, an addition, the increment of `i`, and a compare-and-branch, so about 40 instructions plus the function call. Depending on the core and the compiler, this takes several tens of clock cycles. The hardware needs no clock cycle at all: the module is purely combinational, and the result is valid after the propagation delay of the logic, usually well within one clock period of the surrounding registers.
2. The loop is unrolled at elaboration: the synthesis tool creates a chain of eight adders (and may restructure them into a tree, as long as the function stays the same). The loop variable `i` exists only at compile time, so there is no counter in the hardware. This is why loop bounds in synthesizable code must be constants.
3. The MCU needs eight times as many iterations, so the time grows. The hardware needs eight times as many adders, and wider ones, so the area grows by more than a factor of eight. The result still needs no clock cycle, but the propagation delay grows as well, although an adder tree grows more slowly than a chain. This is the basic trade-off between computing in time and computing in space. Processors often add dedicated hardware for such functions, e.g., the `cpop` instruction of the RISC-V bit-manipulation extension Zbb.
4. Yosys 0.70 reports 26 generic logic cells (`$_XOR_`, `$_NAND_`, `$_ANDNOT_`, and others) and no flip-flops, confirming that the module is purely combinational.
:::

### Synchronous Sequential Design {#sec-sv-sync-design}

The popcount module is purely combinational: its output depends only on its current inputs. Most circuits also need memory, e.g., for the state of a finite state machine (FSM) or the value of a counter. Almost all of them are built as **synchronous sequential circuits** with the structure of @fig-sv-sync-design, which you know from your VHDL courses. A **register** of edge-triggered flip-flops stores the current state. The **next-state logic**, a purely combinational circuit, computes the next state from the current state and the inputs. At every rising clock edge, the register loads the next state from its D input, and the new state appears at its Q output. The outputs of the circuit are derived from the state (Moore FSM) or from the state and the inputs (Mealy FSM).

{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/_fig_sync_design.qmd >}}

Edge-triggered flip-flops are the key to this structure. Their outputs change only at the rising clock edge and stay stable for the rest of the clock period. The next-state logic therefore sees stable inputs for one full clock period, and this is exactly the time it has to compute the next state. The result must have settled before the next rising edge (more precisely, a setup time before it), when the register loads it. The same holds for every path from a register through combinational logic to the next register, so the clock period only has to be longer than the slowest of these paths. Static timing analysis checks exactly this for every path in the design (@sec-sequential). The rule assumes that the inputs also change only after a clock edge, i.e., that they come from registers driven by the same clock. An asynchronous input needs a synchronizer first (@sec-cdc).

In your VHDL designs, you describe this structure with two processes, a register process `reg_proc` and a combinational process such as `next_state_logic`. As a minimal example, consider a toggle flip-flop, whose state inverts at every rising clock edge at which `toggle_i` is high:

```vhdl
-- Register process: only reset and clock in the sensitivity list
reg_proc: process(rst_i, clk_i) is
begin
  if rst_i = '1' then
    state <= '0';
  elsif rising_edge(clk_i) then
    state <= next_state;
  end if;
end process reg_proc;

-- Combinational process: all signals it reads in the sensitivity list
next_state_logic: process(state, toggle_i) is
begin
  -- default assignment
  next_state <= state;

  -- calculate next_state from state and the inputs
  if toggle_i = '1' then
    next_state <= not state;
  end if;
end process next_state_logic;
```

Three rules make this style work:

- The **register process** has only the reset and the clock in its sensitivity list, because the register reacts to nothing else. Its body is always the same: the reset values and, at the rising clock edge, the copies of the `next_` signals. No logic belongs here.
- The sensitivity list of the **combinational process** contains **all signals that are read** in the process. The simulator executes the process only when a signal in this list changes, while the synthesis tool ignores the list (at best with a warning) and builds combinational logic anyway. A missing signal therefore makes the simulation differ from the synthesized hardware. VHDL-2008 avoids this problem with `process(all)`.
- The combinational process starts with a **default assignment**, here `next_state <= state`, followed by all decisions. Every signal is thus assigned on every path, and no latch can arise. Keeping the state is not a latch: the register is the memory, and the next-state logic only feeds the current state back to its D input.

@sec-sv-two-process shows the same style and the same three rules in SystemVerilog.

## The HDL Landscape {#sec-sv-hdl-landscape}

VHDL and Verilog appeared in the 1980s, and for decades they were practically the only choice. In the last fifteen years, a large number of alternatives has appeared, most of them open source. They fall into four families:

1. **Standardized HDLs.** VHDL (IEEE 1076), Verilog (IEEE 1364), and SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800, which absorbed Verilog in 2009) are read directly by the commercial simulation, synthesis, and verification tools. Among the open-source tools, (System)Verilog has much broader support than VHDL (@tbl-sv-vhdl-vs-sv).
2. **Embedded domain-specific languages (eDSLs)**, also called *hardware construction languages*. The hardware is described with a library of a general-purpose language such as Scala, Python, or Haskell. Running the program *generates* the hardware as Verilog, so the classes, functions, loops, and type system of the host language are available to build parameterizable generators.
3. **New standalone HDLs** with their own syntax and compiler, designed to avoid the pitfalls of Verilog. They also emit (System)Verilog.
4. **High-level synthesis (HLS) and compiler intermediate representations.** An algorithm written in C/C++ or a dataflow language is scheduled into clock cycles by the tool, or a compiler uses an intermediate language as its hardware back end.

@tbl-sv-hdl-list gives an overview of the languages you are most likely to come across.

| Language | Family (host language) | Key idea | Origin | Output |
|-----------|---------------|------------------|--------------|----------|
| VHDL | standard, IEEE 1076-2019 | strongly typed, deterministic signal semantics | US Department of Defense, IEEE standard since 1987 | read by commercial tools and GHDL |
| Verilog | standard, IEEE 1364-2005 | weakly typed, compact syntax | Gateway Design Automation, 1984 | read by all tools |
| SystemVerilog | standard, IEEE 1800-2023 | Verilog plus design and verification extensions | Accellera (2002), IEEE since 2005 | read by all tools |
| Chisel | eDSL (Scala) | generators, compiled through FIRRTL and CIRCT | UC Berkeley, 2012 | Verilog, SystemVerilog |
| SpinalHDL | eDSL (Scala) | generators | Charles Papon, 2015 | VHDL, Verilog |
| DFiant (DFHDL) | eDSL (Scala 3) | dataflow, timing-agnostic description | Technion, 2017 | Verilog, VHDL |
| Amaranth | eDSL (Python) | generators, successor of Migen (first called nMigen) | 2019, renamed in 2021 | Verilog via Yosys |
| Migen | eDSL (Python) | generators, still the base of the LiteX SoC builder | M-Labs, 2011 | Verilog |
| PyMTL3 | eDSL (Python) | modeling at functional, cycle, and RTL level | Cornell University, 2014 (as PyMTL) | Verilog |
| PyRTL | eDSL (Python) | minimal RTL for teaching and research | UC Santa Barbara, 2014 | Verilog |
| Magma | eDSL (Python) | strongly typed circuits | Stanford University, 2017 (inactive since 2024) | Verilog via CoreIR |
| Kratos | eDSL (Python) | generators with source-level debugging | Stanford University, 2019 (inactive since 2023) | SystemVerilog |
| HWT | eDSL (Python) | hardware construction library | Michal Orsák, 2015 | VHDL, Verilog, SystemC |
| Clash | eDSL (Haskell) | functional, signals as streams of values | University of Twente, 2009 | VHDL, Verilog, SystemVerilog |
| Hardcaml | eDSL (OCaml) | generators and expect tests | Andy Ray, Jane Street | Verilog, VHDL |
| ROHD | eDSL (Dart) | generator and verification framework | Intel, 2021 | SystemVerilog |
| RHDL | eDSL (Rust) | plain Rust code as hardware description | Samit Basu, 2023 | Verilog |
| Bluespec | standalone | rules as guarded atomic actions | Bluespec Inc., open source since 2020 | Verilog |
| Veryl | standalone | modernized SystemVerilog syntax with formatter, linter, and package manager | 2022 | SystemVerilog |
| Spade | standalone | Rust-like, pipelines as a language construct | Linköping University, 2020 | Verilog |
| Silice | standalone | algorithms, FSMs, and pipelines in a C-like syntax | Sylvain Lefebvre, 2019 | Verilog |
| XLS | HLS (DSLX or C++) | dataflow with automatic pipelining | Google, 2020 | Verilog, SystemVerilog |
| Calyx | compiler IR | intermediate language for accelerator compilers | Cornell University, 2021 | Verilog |
| C/C++ HLS | HLS (C, C++, SystemC) | untimed algorithm, scheduled into cycles by the tool | AMD Vitis HLS, Siemens Catapult, Bambu (open source) | Verilog, VHDL |

: An overview of hardware description languages. Origins and years are those of the first public release. {#tbl-sv-hdl-list}

All non-standard languages have one thing in common: their output is Verilog or SystemVerilog (sometimes VHDL), which then goes through the same simulators and synthesis tools as hand-written RTL. (System)Verilog is the common exchange format of the whole industry. @tbl-sv-hdl-compare compares the four families.

| Criterion | Standardized HDLs | Embedded DSLs | New standalone HDLs | HLS |
|-----------|--------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|
| Industry adoption | very high, the reference for all EDA tools, IP, and jobs | niche, some companies and many open-source cores (Rocket Chip and BOOM in Chisel, VexRiscv in SpinalHDL) | research and early adopters | established for data paths in commercial FPGA and ASIC flows |
| Tool support | all simulators, synthesis, lint, formal, and timing tools | host-language toolchain plus the generated Verilog | one compiler, few other tools | mostly commercial, open-source tools less mature |
| Abstraction and productivity | RTL, limited metaprogramming (parameters, generate) | high, the full host language builds generators | medium to high, modern syntax and type inference | highest, algorithmic description |
| Learning curve | moderate, Verilog has many pitfalls | host language plus hardware thinking | new syntax, small community and documentation | low for software developers, but good results need hardware knowledge and tool directives |
| Error checking | VHDL strongly typed, (System)Verilog weakly typed and dependent on lint | type systems of the host languages catch many errors | strong type systems, some prevent whole classes of bugs (e.g., races in Bluespec) | depends on the C model, timing is implicit |
| Debugging | source, waveform, and netlist correspond directly | generated Verilog with machine-made names | similar to eDSLs | the RTL is hard to relate to the source, latency depends on scheduling |
| Long-term risk | decades of stability | depends on small projects, several are dormant | early stage | lock-in to a vendor tool |

: Comparison of the HDL families {#tbl-sv-hdl-compare}

### Why SystemVerilog in This Course {#sec-sv-why}

- **Industry standard.** SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800-2023 [@IEEE_1800_2023]) is the dominant language for ASIC design and verification. Every EDA tool, IP vendor, and foundry flow supports it.
- **Open-source tool support.** All tools of our flow read it: the simulators Verilator and Icarus Verilog (also under cocotb), Yosys and LibreLane, slang, and Verible. The AMS chip template (@sec-intro-template) is written in SystemVerilog.
- **You have to read it anyway.** Netlists, gate-level simulations, and the output of every alternative HDL are (System)Verilog. Debugging always ends there. @sec-sv-verilog shows how plain Verilog maps onto SystemVerilog.
- **cocotb for verification.** The verification part of SystemVerilog (classes and constrained randomization) and the UVM library built on it form a large field of their own. With cocotb (@sec-verification), we write testbenches in Python and use SystemVerilog mainly for the synthesizable RTL.
- **A good foundation.** With solid RTL skills in SystemVerilog, you can learn an embedded DSL such as Chisel or Amaranth later with little extra effort, since it describes the same registers and logic.

### VHDL versus SystemVerilog {#sec-sv-vhdl-vs-sv}

@tbl-sv-vhdl-vs-sv compares the two languages.

| Aspect | VHDL | SystemVerilog |
|----------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Standard | IEEE 1076-2019 | IEEE 1800-2023, includes Verilog |
| Typing | strong, explicit conversions (`numeric_std`) | weak, widths are extended or truncated silently, lint catches part of it |
| Verbosity | verbose (entity and architecture, type conversions) | compact |
| Case sensitivity | case-insensitive | case-sensitive (`clk` and `Clk` are different) |
| Simulation semantics | signals update after a delta cycle, the order of processes never matters | blocking and non-blocking assignments, races are possible if the coding rules are broken |
| Verification features | libraries (OSVVM, UVVM) | built in: classes, randomization, assertions (SVA), coverage, plus the UVM class library (IEEE 1800.2) |
| Typical use | FPGA, aerospace and defense, Europe, academia | ASIC design and verification worldwide |
| Open-source tools | GHDL (simulation), experimental synthesis via a Yosys plugin | Verilator, Icarus Verilog, Yosys, slang, Verible |

: VHDL versus SystemVerilog {#tbl-sv-vhdl-vs-sv}

In short, VHDL protects you with strong typing, while SystemVerilog relies on coding discipline and on the linter. The rest of this chapter is about that discipline.

## Cheat-Sheets, Guidelines, and Further Reading {#sec-sv-references}

Besides the SystemVerilog cheat-sheet in the appendix of this book (@sec-app-sv-cheatsheet), two cheat-sheets are provided with the AMS chip template:

- [SystemVerilog Cheat-Sheet](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13cmos5l-ams-chip-template/blob/main/doc/verilog/SystemVerilog_cheatsheet.pdf) (S. H. Shawon, Algo Science Lab)
- [Verilog Cheat-Sheet](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13cmos5l-ams-chip-template/blob/main/doc/verilog/Verilog_cheatsheet.pdf) (S. Winberg and J. Taylor)

::: {.callout-warning title="Using the Cheat-Sheets"}
Both cheat-sheets are syntax references, not style guides. The SystemVerilog cheat-sheet also covers the verification part of the language (classes, randomization, interfaces, assertions), and not all of its examples are synthesizable or accepted by the open-source tools of our flow. The Verilog cheat-sheet describes plain Verilog-2001 with `reg`, `wire`, and `always @(...)`, for which we use the SystemVerilog constructs of this chapter instead (@sec-sv-verilog). Whatever you copy, lint it with Verilator and check it with a quick Yosys synthesis (@sec-sv-tools).
:::

For HDL coding guidelines, read the [Circuit Designer's Etiquette](https://iic-jku.github.io/analog-circuit-design/aicd.html#prolog) of the Analog Circuit Design course, in particular its section [VHDL/Verilog Coding Guide](https://iic-jku.github.io/analog-circuit-design/aicd.html#vhdlverilog-coding-guide). @sec-sv-guidelines summarizes its rules for SystemVerilog. The etiquette recommends the detailed [lowRISC Verilog Coding Style Guide](https://github.com/lowRISC/style-guides/blob/master/VerilogCodingStyle.md) [@lowRISC_Style_Guide], from which this course takes most of its naming conventions.

::: {.callout-note title="Further Reading"}
- The SystemVerilog standard IEEE 1800-2023 [@IEEE_1800_2023] is the final reference. It is available free of charge through the IEEE GET Program ([announcement by Accellera](https://accellera.org/news/press-releases/394-accellera-announces-ieee-1800-2023-standard-available-through-ieee-get-program)).
- [@Harris_Harris_2021] shows SystemVerilog and VHDL side by side for all basic building blocks, which helps with the transition.
- [@Sutherland_2017] covers RTL modeling with SystemVerilog for simulation and synthesis in depth.
- [@Sutherland_Mills_2007] collects 101 common coding errors in Verilog and SystemVerilog and how to avoid them.
:::

## SystemVerilog for VHDL Designers {#sec-sv-basics}

@tbl-sv-rosetta maps the most important VHDL constructs onto SystemVerilog. The following sections go through them one by one. Where a VHDL version helps, it comes first, and the sequential designs use the two-process style you know from your VHDL courses.

| Concept | VHDL | SystemVerilog |
|------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Design unit | `entity` + `architecture` | `module ... endmodule` |
| Generic / parameter | `WIDTH : positive := 8` | `parameter int unsigned WIDTH = 8` |
| Constant | `constant C_LAST : natural := 9;` | `localparam int unsigned LAST = 9;` |
| Port | `a_i : in std_logic_vector(7 downto 0)` | `input logic [7:0] a_i` |
| Bit, vector | `std_logic`, `std_logic_vector` | `logic`, `logic [N-1:0]` |
| Unsigned, signed | `unsigned`, `signed` (`numeric_std`) | `logic [N-1:0]` (unsigned), `logic signed [N-1:0]` |
| All zeros | `(others => '0')` | `'0` |
| Concatenation | `a & b` | `{a, b}` |
| Concurrent assignment | `y <= a and b;` | `assign y = a & b;` |
| Conditional assignment | `y <= a when s = '1' else b;` | `assign y = s ? a : b;` |
| Combinational process | `process(a, b)` (VHDL-2008: `process(all)`) | `always_comb` |
| Register process | `process(rst_i, clk_i)` with `rising_edge(clk_i)` | `always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni)` |
| Signal assignment in the register process | `q <= d;` | `q <= d;` (non-blocking) |
| Variable assignment | `v := a;` | `v = a;` (blocking) |
| Enumeration | `type t_state is (IDLE, RUN, DONE);` | `typedef enum logic [1:0] {StIdle, StRun, StDone} state_e;` |
| Record | `type t_x is record ... end record;` | `typedef struct packed { ... } x_t;` |
| Package | `package ... end package;`, `use work.pkg.all;` | `package ... endpackage`, `pkg::NAME` |
| Instance | `adder_0: entity work.adder port map(...)` | `adder adder_0 (...);` |
| Generate | `gen: for i in 0 to 3 generate` | `for (genvar i = 0; i < 4; i++) begin : gen` |
| Width of a constant | `natural(ceil(log2(real(N))))` | `$clog2(N)` |
| Comment | `--` | `//` and `/* ... */` |

: Mapping of VHDL constructs onto SystemVerilog {#tbl-sv-rosetta}

### Modules, Ports, and Parameters {#sec-sv-modules}

An unsigned adder with a generic width and a carry bit is a good first example. In VHDL, it needs an entity, an architecture, three type conversions, and a `resize`:

```{.vhdl filename="adder/vhdl/adder_ea.vhd"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/adder/vhdl/adder_ea.vhd >}}
```

In SystemVerilog, a single `module` replaces entity and architecture:

```{.systemverilog filename="adder/rtl/adder.sv"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/adder/rtl/adder.sv >}}
```

- **Parameters** are declared in the `#( ... )` list before the ports, like generics. The type `int unsigned` makes the parameter a non-negative 32-bit integer. Constants that must not be changed from outside are `localparam`s.
- **Ports** are declared in the module header (ANSI style) with direction, type, width, and name. We use the suffixes `_i`, `_o`, and `_io` for inputs, outputs, and bidirectional ports.
- **No type conversions.** SystemVerilog has no separate types for bit vectors and numbers, so `+` works directly on `logic` vectors. The concatenations `{1'b0, a_i}` and `{1'b0, b_i}` make the extension to `WIDTH+1` bits explicit. The carry would be kept without them as well, since the target is `WIDTH+1` bits wide (@sec-sv-operators), but the explicit version states the intent.
- **Case sensitivity.** Unlike VHDL, SystemVerilog is case-sensitive: `Clk` and `clk` are two different signals. Write signals in lowercase snake_case and parameters in UPPERCASE.
- **`` `default_nettype none``** at the top of the file makes an undeclared name an error. Without it, Verilog silently creates a 1-bit wire for a misspelled name on the left side of an `assign` or in a port connection. The `` `default_nettype wire`` at the end restores the default for files compiled afterwards.
- **One module per file**, and the file name equals the module name (`adder.sv`). Pass all files to the tools as a list instead of pulling modules in with `` `include ``, so that the list shows every file of the design and no module is read twice. Even in a list, a `` `define`` stays active for all files that follow, in every tool. Icarus Verilog also keeps `` `default_nettype``, while Verilator and Yosys reset it for each file. Ending every file with `` `default_nettype wire`` gives the same result in all tools.

### Data Types and Literals {#sec-sv-types}

The everyday type of SystemVerilog is `logic`. It has four values: `0`, `1`, `x` (unknown), and `z` (high impedance). VHDL's `std_logic` has nine values, but the four that matter in RTL map directly. As in VHDL, where an uninitialized `std_logic` is `'U'`, a `logic` that is never assigned or reset is `x` in a four-state simulator such as Icarus Verilog, so a missing reset stays visible in the waveform. Verilator is a two-state simulator for speed and replaces `x` with `0` or a random value, which is one reason to simulate with both.

- **Use `logic` for every signal in RTL.** A `logic` variable assigned in an `always_comb` block, an `always_ff` block, or by an `assign` must not be assigned anywhere else. Verilator reports a second driver as a `MULTIDRIVEN` warning. Icarus Verilog reports an error only if one of the drivers is an `assign`, and it accepts two `always_comb` or two `always_ff` blocks without a message. The single-driver rule corresponds to the unresolved `std_ulogic` in VHDL, not to the resolved `std_logic`, which allows several drivers. Nets with several drivers (tri-state buses) need the type `wire` and only appear at the pads of an ASIC.
- **`wire` and `reg` are legacy Verilog.** Despite its name, `reg` does not mean register. Whether a flip-flop is created depends only on how a variable is assigned, never on its type.
- **Vectors** are declared as `logic [7:0] data`, like `std_logic_vector(7 downto 0)` with the MSB on the left. Select a bit with `data[0]`, a fixed range with `data[7:4]`, and a range at a variable position with `data[i*4 +: 4]` (four bits starting at bit `i*4`).
- **Signedness.** Vectors are unsigned by default, `logic signed [15:0] acc` declares a signed one, and `$signed()` and `$unsigned()` convert. If only one operand of an expression is unsigned, the whole expression is evaluated unsigned, so do not mix them.
- **Two-state types** such as `bit`, `int` (32 bits, signed), and `int unsigned` know only `0` and `1`. Use them for parameters, loop variables, and in testbenches, but not for RTL signals, where they would turn an `x` into a `0` and hide bugs.
- **Arrays.** A *packed* array `logic [3:0][7:0] word` is a 32-bit vector made of four bytes and can be used as one vector. An *unpacked* array `logic [7:0] mem [16]` holds 16 separate bytes, e.g., a register file.

Literals carry their width in front of the base, as @tbl-sv-literals shows. Always size your literals, because an unsized number such as `20` is a 32-bit integer.

| SystemVerilog | VHDL | Meaning |
|--------------|------------------|------------------|
| `8'b1010_0101` | `"10100101"` | 8-bit binary, `_` only improves readability |
| `8'hA5` | `x"A5"` | 8-bit hexadecimal |
| `8'd165` | `std_logic_vector(to_unsigned(165, 8))` | 8-bit decimal |
| `'0`, `'1` | `(others => '0')`, `(others => '1')` | all bits zero or one, for any width |
| `'x`, `'z` | `(others => 'X')`, `(others => 'Z')` | all bits unknown or high impedance |
| `4'b10x1` | `"10X1"` | literal with an unknown bit |
| `165` | `165` | unsized: a 32-bit signed integer |

: Literals in SystemVerilog and VHDL {#tbl-sv-literals}

### Operators and Expression Widths {#sec-sv-operators}

Most operators exist in both languages, but SystemVerilog uses the C notation (@tbl-sv-operators).

+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| VHDL                            | SystemVerilog             | Meaning                                                            |
+=================================+===========================+====================================================================+
| `not a`                         | `~a`                      | bitwise NOT                                                        |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `a and b`, `a or b`, `a xor b`  | `a & b`, `a | b`, `a ^ b` | bitwise AND, OR, XOR                                               |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `and a` (VHDL-2008 only)        | `&a`, `|a`, `^a`          | reduction: AND, OR, XOR (parity) of all bits, 1-bit result         |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `not`, `and`, `or` on `boolean` | `!a`, `a && b`, `a || b`  | logical operators, 1-bit result                                    |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `=`, `/=`                       | `==`, `!=`                | equality, `x` if an `x` or `z` bit makes the result ambiguous      |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| none                            | `===`, `!==`              | case equality, compares `x` and `z` literally, only in testbenches |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`            | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`      | relational (`<=` is also the non-blocking assignment)              |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `+`, `-`, `*`                   | `+`, `-`, `*`             | arithmetic                                                         |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `shift_left()`, `shift_right()` | `<<`, `>>`                | logical shift                                                      |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `shift_right()` on `signed`     | `>>>`                     | arithmetic shift, only for signed operands                         |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `a & b`                         | `{a, b}`                  | concatenation                                                      |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| none                            | `{4{a}}`                  | replication: `a` four times                                        |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `a when s = '1' else b`         | `s ? a : b`               | conditional operator                                               |
+---------------------------------+---------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Operators in VHDL and SystemVerilog {#tbl-sv-operators}

The biggest difference from VHDL is how widths are handled. In SystemVerilog, the operands of an expression are extended to the width of the widest operand *and of the assignment target*, and the result is then truncated to the target. Nothing is reported as an error:

```systemverilog
logic [7:0] a, b, sum8;
logic [8:0] sum9;
logic [3:0] nibble, count;
logic       hit;

assign sum8   = a + b;          // carry silently lost, no warning
assign sum9   = a + b;          // carry kept, the target is 9 bits wide
assign nibble = a;              // MSBs cut off (Verilator: WIDTHTRUNC)
assign hit    = (count == 20);  // always false (Verilator: WIDTHEXPAND)
```

In VHDL, `sum9 <= a + b` and `nibble <= a` are length mismatches: GHDL already warns about `nibble <= a` during the analysis and stops the simulation with a bound check failure. `sum8` loses the carry in both languages. Verilator reports the truncation and the comparison with a constant that does not fit, but not the lost carry. So think about the width of every arithmetic result, and make extensions explicit with a concatenation such as `{1'b0, a}` or a size cast such as `9'(a)`.

### Concurrent Assignments {#sec-sv-assign}

The VHDL concurrent signal assignment becomes an `assign` statement, a *continuous assignment* that is re-evaluated whenever one of its operands changes:

```systemverilog
// VHDL: y_o <= a_i and b_i;
assign y_o   = a_i & b_i;

// VHDL: mux_o <= a_i when sel_i = '1' else b_i;
assign mux_o = sel_i ? a_i : b_i;
```

A selected signal assignment (`with ... select`) becomes a `case` statement in an `always_comb` block (@sec-sv-case). Unlike VHDL-93, SystemVerilog lets you read an output port inside the module, so the internal copy of an output that VHDL needs is not necessary.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: A 4:1 Multiplexer in SystemVerilog"}
The following VHDL entity is a 4:1 multiplexer for 8-bit data with a zero flag:

```{.vhdl filename="mux4/vhdl/mux4_ea.vhd"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/mux4/vhdl/mux4_ea.vhd >}}
```

1. Translate it into a SystemVerilog module `mux4` with the same port names and save it as `mux4.sv`. @sec-sv-case shows the syntax of the `case` statement.
2. Lint your module in the container with `verilator --lint-only -Wall mux4.sv` (@sec-sv-tools-lint explains the command). Verilator must not report any warning.
:::

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution: A 4:1 Multiplexer in SystemVerilog" collapse="true"}
```{.systemverilog filename="mux4/rtl/mux4.sv"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/mux4/rtl/mux4.sv >}}
```

- The selected signal assignment becomes a `case` statement in `always_comb`, and `when others` becomes `default`. A chain of conditional operators `?:` in an `assign` is also correct.
- `x"00"` becomes `8'h00`. The comparison already has a 1-bit result, so `'1' when ... else '0'` is not needed.
- The output `y_o` is read directly, and the internal signal `y` of the VHDL version is gone.
- The zero flag can also be written with the reduction NOR operator, `assign zero_o = ~|y_o;`.
:::

### Processes: `always_comb`, `always_ff`, and `always_latch` {#sec-sv-processes}

SystemVerilog has three dedicated process types for synthesizable code, which replace the general-purpose `always` block of Verilog:

- **`always_comb`** describes combinational logic. It is sensitive to every signal it reads, like `process(all)` in VHDL-2008, so the sensitivity list can never be incomplete. The tools also check that the block is really combinational: if a variable is not assigned on every path, Verilator warns (`LATCH`) and Yosys stops with an error.
- **`always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni)`** describes flip-flops. Its event list contains only the clock edge and, for an asynchronous reset, the reset edge.
- **`always_latch`** describes an intended latch, which you will rarely need.

Within these blocks, SystemVerilog has two kinds of assignments, which correspond to the variables and signals of VHDL:

- The **blocking assignment** `=` updates the variable immediately, and the next statement already sees the new value, like a VHDL variable (`:=`).
- The **non-blocking assignment** `<=` evaluates the right-hand side immediately but updates the variable only after all blocks triggered by the same clock edge have read their inputs, like a VHDL signal assignment.

The difference matters as soon as a register reads another register that is updated at the same clock edge. The following two registers swap their values at every clock edge:

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk_i) begin
  a_q <= b_q;
  b_q <= a_q;  // reads the old value of a_q: a real swap
end
```

With blocking assignments in this block, `b_q` would read the *new* value of `a_q`, and both registers would end up with the old value of `b_q`, in simulation and in synthesis. It gets worse when the two blocking assignments sit in two separate `always_ff` blocks. The simulation result then depends on the order in which the simulator runs the blocks, which the standard leaves open, while synthesis builds the swap anyway. Icarus Verilog 14 and Verilator 5.052 both show no swap for this case, while the netlist of Yosys swaps. This mismatch between simulation and synthesis is one of the most common SystemVerilog bugs, and the following rules avoid it.

::: {.callout-important title="The Golden Rules of Processes"}
1. In `always_ff`, use only non-blocking assignments `<=`.
2. In `always_comb`, use only blocking assignments `=`.
3. Assign every variable in exactly one block (or one `assign`).
4. Never use the plain `always` block or `initial` in RTL, only `always_comb`, `always_ff`, and `always_latch`.
:::

### Registers and Resets {#sec-sv-registers}

In your VHDL style, every register process has an active-high asynchronous reset (@sec-sv-sync-design). In SystemVerilog, the three register variants you need look as follows:

```systemverilog
// Asynchronous active-low reset (the default in this course)
always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
  if (!rst_ni) begin
    q <= '0;
  end else begin
    q <= d;
  end
end

// Synchronous active-high reset (counter of the AMS chip template)
always_ff @(posedge clk_i) begin
  if (reset_i) begin
    q <= '0;
  end else begin
    q <= d;
  end
end

// No reset (pure data path registers)
always_ff @(posedge clk_i) begin
  q <= d;
end
```

In this course, the default is an **asynchronous active-low reset** named `rst_ni` (`_n` for active low, `_i` for input). This is the common convention in ASIC design and the rule of the lowRISC style guide. It also matches the hardware: the reset flip-flops of the SG13CMOS5L standard-cell library, e.g., `sg13cmos5l_dfrbp_1` and `sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1`, have an active-low reset pin `RESET_B`, and the reset pad of a chip is usually active low (`rst_n` in the chip core of the AMS chip template). Synthesis handles either polarity: an active-high reset only costs an inverter.

- The reset test must be the first statement in the block, and its polarity must match the event list (`negedge rst_ni` with `if (!rst_ni)`). Otherwise, the block cannot be mapped onto a flip-flop with an asynchronous reset.
- An asynchronous reset may be asserted at any time, but it must be released synchronously to the clock with a reset synchronizer (@sec-cdc).
- A synchronous reset is ordinary logic in front of the D input of a flip-flop without reset.
- A clock enable, written as `end else if (en_i) begin q <= d; end`, keeps the old value when `en_i` is low. The synthesis tool maps it onto a flip-flop with an enable input or a multiplexer in front of D. This is a register, not a latch.

### The Two-Process Style {#sec-sv-two-process}

In your VHDL designs, you split each block into a register process (`reg_proc`), which only holds the reset values and copies the `next_` signals into the registers, and one or more combinational processes, which start with complete default assignments and contain all decisions (@sec-sv-sync-design). This style maps one to one onto SystemVerilog, and we keep it: `always_ff` is the register process, `always_comb` the combinational process, and the VHDL pair `next_state` and `state` becomes `state_d` (the next value at the D input of the register in @fig-sv-sync-design) and `state_q` (the current value at its Q output), as in the lowRISC style guide. Here is the toggle flip-flop of @sec-sv-sync-design in SystemVerilog:

```systemverilog
// Register process: only clock and reset in the event list
always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
  if (!rst_ni) begin
    state_q <= 1'b0;
  end else begin
    state_q <= state_d;
  end
end

// Combinational process: the sensitivity list is inferred
always_comb begin
  // default assignment
  state_d = state_q;

  // calculate state_d from state_q and the inputs
  if (toggle_i) begin
    state_d = ~state_q;
  end
end
```

The three rules of the VHDL style carry over. `always_comb` makes the second one unnecessary, and the tools check the other two:

- The event list of `always_ff` contains only the clock edge and the reset edge, just like the sensitivity list of `reg_proc`. If you add a data signal to it, Yosys stops with an error, even though Verilator accepts it.
- `always_comb` infers the complete sensitivity list by itself, so a forgotten signal is no longer possible.
- The default assignment `state_d = state_q;` comes first, as in VHDL. If you forget it, the tools report the latch: Verilator warns, and Yosys stops with an error (@sec-sv-case).

The register process uses non-blocking assignments `<=` and the combinational process blocking assignments `=`, as the Golden Rules of @sec-sv-processes demand. The order of the two blocks in the file does not matter, since both are concurrent. This snippet follows the order of the VHDL version, while the files of this chapter put `always_comb` first, following the data flow from the logic into the register. Yosys 0.70 synthesizes the toggle flip-flop into exactly two cells, an inverter and a flip-flop with enable (`$_DFFE_PN0P_`) whose enable input is `toggle_i`. The default assignment that keeps the state has become the enable of the flip-flop, not a latch.

As a larger example, consider a tick generator: while `en_i` is high, `tick_o` is high for one clock cycle every `DIV` clock cycles. Such a one-cycle pulse is a *strobe*, which typically triggers other blocks, e.g., to restart a counter or to signal that a result is valid. Here is the VHDL version in the style you know:

```{.vhdl filename="tick_gen/vhdl/tick_gen_ea.vhd"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/tick_gen/vhdl/tick_gen_ea.vhd >}}
```

And the same design in SystemVerilog:

```{.systemverilog filename="tick_gen/rtl/tick_gen.sv"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/tick_gen/rtl/tick_gen.sv >}}
```

@tbl-sv-two-process lists the correspondences. With the default `DIV = 10`, both versions describe the same hardware apart from the reset polarity: four flip-flops for the counter, one for the tick, and the increment and compare logic in front of them. The VHDL and SystemVerilog versions of the tick generator and of the two FSMs of this chapter were simulated with the same cocotb testbenches, with the reset adapted, to make sure they behave identically.

| VHDL (two-process) | SystemVerilog (two-process) |
|-------------------------|-------------------------|
| `reg_proc: process(rst_i, clk_i)` | `always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni)` |
| `counter_logic: process(count, en_i)` | `always_comb` (complete sensitivity, inferred) |
| `count`, `next_count` | `count_q`, `count_d` |
| `if rst_i = '1' then` (active high) | `if (!rst_ni)` (active low) |
| `natural(ceil(log2(real(DIV))))` | `$clog2(DIV)` |
| `to_unsigned(DIV - 1, C_COUNT_WIDTH)` | `COUNT_WIDTH'(DIV - 1)` (size cast) |
| `(others => '0')` | `'0` |
| `count + 1` | `count_q + 1'b1` |
| `tick_o <= tick;` | `assign tick_o = tick_q;` |

: The two-process style in VHDL and SystemVerilog {#tbl-sv-two-process}

The two-process style has three advantages. The register process is a fixed template that you never have to think about again. The defaults at the top of the combinational process make latches impossible. And the next values (`_d`) are signals that you can inspect in the waveform and reuse in other logic. The single-process style, in which the next-state logic is written directly into `always_ff` (as in the counter of the AMS chip template, @sec-sv-template), is fine for simple registers and counters, and both styles synthesize to the same hardware. We recommend the two-process style whenever the next-state logic is more than a line or two, and always for FSMs.

### `if`, `case`, and Latches {#sec-sv-case}

`if`, `else if`, and `else` work as `if`, `elsif`, and `else` in VHDL and describe a priority. Unlike in VHDL, a condition does not need to be of type `boolean`: every nonzero value is true, so you write `if (en_i)` instead of `if en_i = '1' then`. The `case` statement works as in VHDL, with `default` instead of `when others`. There are two important differences:

- VHDL requires a `case` to cover all values, but SystemVerilog does not. A missing value in an `always_comb` block leaves the variable unassigned for that value, and the tools infer a **latch** that holds the old value.
- The qualifier **`unique`** in `unique case` states that exactly one item matches at a time, so the items can be implemented as a parallel multiplexer instead of a priority chain. Simulators that support it report a violation at run time. Icarus Verilog prints a "sorry" message that it ignores the qualifier, but it still warns at run time when no item matches. It does not check for overlapping items. Use `unique case` together with a `default` item.

For decoders, `casez` treats `?` in the case items as don't care, e.g., `4'b01??`. Avoid `casex`, which also treats an `x` in the case expression as don't care and thereby hides `x` values in simulation.

A latch appears whenever a combinational block does not assign a variable on every path:

```systemverilog
// Latch: y_o keeps its old value while en_i is low
always_comb begin
  if (en_i) y_o = a_i;
end

// Fixed: default assignment first, then the decisions
always_comb begin
  y_o = '0;
  if (en_i) y_o = a_i;
end
```

In a synchronous design, latches are almost always a bug: static timing analysis treats them differently from flip-flops (@sec-sequential), they pass glitches, and they complicate the scan test (@sec-dft). The SG13CMOS5L library contains latch cells (e.g., `sg13cmos5l_dlhq_1`), so an unintended latch synthesizes without complaint if nobody checks. Here `always_comb` pays off: for the plain Verilog block `always @(*)`, Yosys 0.70 only prints a warning and builds the latches, while it stops with an error for `always_comb`. If you really need a latch, write it with `always_latch`, so that your intention is documented.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: Let the Linter Find the Bugs"}
The following module is meant to be a small ALU with a registered result: `op_i` selects addition (`00`), subtraction (`01`), bitwise AND (`10`), or bitwise OR (`11`). `result_o` is the registered result, `zero_o` is high when `result_o` is zero, and the register has an asynchronous active-low reset. The file contains several mistakes.

```{.systemverilog filename="lint_me/exercise/lint_me.sv"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/lint_me/exercise/lint_me.sv >}}
```

1. Save the file as `lint_me.sv` and lint it with `verilator --lint-only -Wall lint_me.sv`. Explain every warning.
2. Synthesize the file with `yosys -p "read_verilog -sv lint_me.sv; synth -top lint_me; stat"`. What does Yosys report?
3. Fix the code until Verilator reports no warning, and synthesize it again. Which cells hold the result?
:::

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution: Let the Linter Find the Bugs" collapse="true"}
Verilator 5.052 reports seven warnings and exits with an error:

- `IMPLICIT`: the name `zero` is not declared, so Verilog creates an implicit 1-bit wire. It is a typo for `zero_o`.
- `UNDRIVEN` for `zero_o` and `UNUSEDSIGNAL` for `zero`: two consequences of the same typo.
- `BLKSEQ` (twice): blocking assignments `=` in the `always_ff` block, which must be non-blocking `<=`.
- `CASEINCOMPLETE`: the case does not cover `op_i = 2'b11`, the OR operation was forgotten.
- `LATCH` for `alu`: because of the missing case item, `alu` keeps its old value for `op_i = 2'b11`.

The corrected module fixes the typo, adds `` `default_nettype none``, which would have turned it into an error, completes the case with `unique` and a `default`, and uses non-blocking assignments:

```{.systemverilog filename="lint_me/rtl/lint_me.sv"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/lint_me/rtl/lint_me.sv >}}
```

For the original file, Yosys warns that `zero` is implicitly declared and then stops with ``ERROR: Latch inferred for signal `\lint_me.\alu' from always_comb process``. The fixed version synthesizes to 114 generic cells, among them eight `$_DFF_PN0_` cells for `result_q`: flip-flops on the positive clock edge (`P`) with an active-low reset (`N`) to zero (`0`).
:::

### Finite State Machines {#sec-sv-fsm}

FSMs are where the two-process style pays off most. As an example, consider a simple controller: a `start_i` pulse moves it from idle to a run state, in which `busy_o` is high, until `last_i` is high. Then `done_o` is high for one clock cycle, and the FSM returns to idle. Both outputs depend only on the state (Moore FSM). In VHDL:

```{.vhdl filename="ctrl_fsm/vhdl/ctrl_fsm_ea.vhd"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/ctrl_fsm/vhdl/ctrl_fsm_ea.vhd >}}
```

In SystemVerilog:

```{.systemverilog filename="ctrl_fsm/rtl/ctrl_fsm.sv"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/ctrl_fsm/rtl/ctrl_fsm.sv >}}
```

- The state type is a `typedef enum` with an explicit base type (`logic [1:0]`). Following the lowRISC style guide, the type name ends in `_e` and the state names are UpperCamelCase with the prefix `St`.
- In VHDL, a `case` over an enumeration type with three values is complete. The 2-bit state of the SystemVerilog version has a fourth encoding, `2'b11`, which the `default` item sends back to idle.
- As in VHDL, the next state defaults to the current state, and every output defaults to its inactive value before the `case`.
- The synthesis tool is free to choose the state encoding. Yosys 0.70 recognizes this FSM and re-encodes it one-hot, with three flip-flops instead of two.
- Write the transitions with `if` and `else`. A conditional operator between enumeration values, such as `state_d = start_i ? StRun : StIdle;`, is rejected by Icarus Verilog 14, which requires an explicit cast for it.

### Hierarchy and Generate {#sec-sv-hierarchy}

An instance of the adder of @sec-sv-modules with a width of 16 bits looks as follows in VHDL:

```vhdl
adder_0: entity work.adder
  generic map(
    WIDTH => 16
  )
  port map(
    a_i => x,
    b_i => y,
    sum_o => s
  );
```

And in SystemVerilog:

```systemverilog
adder #(
  .WIDTH(16)
) adder_0 (
  .a_i  (x),
  .b_i  (y),
  .sum_o(s)
);
```

Always connect parameters and ports by name, never by position, and connect every port. Avoid the shortcuts `.*` and `.name`, which connect ports implicitly to signals of the same name and make the code hard to review.

A `for` loop outside a process is a generate loop, which creates hardware once per iteration:

```vhdl
gen_lane: for i in 0 to 3 generate
  adder_i: entity work.adder
    generic map(
      WIDTH => 8
    )
    port map(
      a_i => lane_a(i),
      b_i => lane_b(i),
      sum_o => lane_sum(i)
    );
end generate gen_lane;
```

```systemverilog
logic [3:0][7:0] lane_a, lane_b;
logic [3:0][8:0] lane_sum;

for (genvar i = 0; i < 4; i++) begin : gen_lane
  adder #(
    .WIDTH(8)
  ) adder_i (
    .a_i  (lane_a[i]),
    .b_i  (lane_b[i]),
    .sum_o(lane_sum[i])
  );
end
```

The name of the block (`gen_lane`) becomes part of the hierarchical instance names, e.g., `gen_lane[2].adder_i`. Similarly, `if (PARAM) begin : gen_name ... end` outside a process creates hardware only if the parameter is true.

### Packages, Typedefs, and Functions {#sec-sv-packages}

A `package` collects constants, types, and functions that several modules share, like a VHDL package:

```{.systemverilog filename="alu_pkg.sv"}
package alu_pkg;

  localparam int unsigned DATA_WIDTH = 8;

  typedef enum logic [1:0] {
    OpAdd,
    OpSub,
    OpAnd,
    OpOr
  } alu_op_e;

  typedef struct packed {
    alu_op_e               op;
    logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] operand;
  } instr_t;

  function automatic logic is_zero(input logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] data);
    is_zero = (data == '0);
  endfunction

endpackage
```

A module refers to the package contents with the scope operator `::`, and the package file must be compiled before the modules that use it:

```systemverilog
module alu (
  input  logic [alu_pkg::DATA_WIDTH-1:0] a_i,
  input  alu_pkg::instr_t                instr_i,
  output logic [alu_pkg::DATA_WIDTH-1:0] result_o,
  output logic                           zero_o
);

  always_comb begin
    unique case (instr_i.op)
      alu_pkg::OpAdd: result_o = a_i + instr_i.operand;
      alu_pkg::OpSub: result_o = a_i - instr_i.operand;
      alu_pkg::OpAnd: result_o = a_i & instr_i.operand;
      default:        result_o = a_i | instr_i.operand;
    endcase
  end

  assign zero_o = alu_pkg::is_zero(result_o);

endmodule
```

- A `typedef struct packed` replaces a VHDL record. Its fields are accessed with a dot (`instr_i.op`), and the whole struct is also a plain bit vector, so it can be used as a port or stored in a register.
- A `function automatic` describes combinational logic, and every call becomes a separate copy of that logic. Declare functions `automatic`, so that every call gets its own variables. Tasks, which may contain timing, belong in testbenches.

::: {.callout-important title="Tool Support for SystemVerilog Features"}
The default SystemVerilog front end of Yosys, which LibreLane uses unless `USE_SLANG: True` is set in its configuration, supports only part of the language. In Yosys 0.70, it fails on three constructs that Verilator and Icarus Verilog accept: `import alu_pkg::*` (the counterpart of `use work.alu_pkg.all`), `return` statements in functions, and unpacked arrays as ports. An `import` inside the module or its header gives a syntax error, and one before the `module` keyword gives a syntax error or an internal error. The code of this chapter therefore uses the scope operator `pkg::NAME`, assigns a function result to the function name, and uses packed arrays at ports. The slang front end of Yosys (`read_slang`, enabled in LibreLane with `USE_SLANG: True`) accepts all of these constructs. For the same reason, the counter of the AMS chip template uses `` `define`` macros instead of a package. When you use struct fields inside `always_comb`, Icarus Verilog prints a "sorry" message that the block becomes sensitive to the whole struct, which does not change the result.
:::

### What Is Synthesizable {#sec-sv-synthesizable}

Synthesis understands only a subset of SystemVerilog. Everything else is for simulation and testbenches only (@tbl-sv-synthesizable).

| Synthesizable (RTL) | Simulation and testbenches only |
|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| `module`, `parameter`, `localparam`, `assign` | `initial` blocks (FPGA tools accept them for register initialization, ASICs have no initial values, use a reset) |
| `always_comb`, `always_ff`, `always_latch` | delays (`#10`), event waits inside procedural code (`@(...)`, `wait`) |
| `if`, `case`, `for` loops with constant bounds | system tasks such as `$display`, `$finish`, `$fatal`, `$dumpvars` |
| `function automatic`, generate loops and conditions | `===` and `!==`, `real`, `string` |
| `typedef enum`, `typedef struct packed`, packed arrays, packages | classes, `randomize()`, `fork` and `join`, tasks with timing |
| `+`, `-`, `*`, shifts, comparisons on vectors | loops whose number of iterations depends on data |

: The synthesizable subset of SystemVerilog {#tbl-sv-synthesizable}

Be careful with `/` and `%`: they synthesize to large and slow logic unless the divisor is a constant power of two, in which case they reduce to a shift or a bit selection.

### Verilog versus SystemVerilog {#sec-sv-verilog}

SystemVerilog grew out of Verilog. Verilog became the IEEE standard 1364 in 1995, was revised in 2001 and 2005, and was merged into SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800) in 2009. SystemVerilog is therefore a superset of Verilog: a Verilog file is also valid SystemVerilog, unless it uses one of the new keywords, such as `logic` or `bit`, as a name. In this course, you write SystemVerilog, but you will read plain Verilog all the time:

- **Netlists.** Yosys and LibreLane write their netlists in plain Verilog, e.g., `final/nl/counter_top.nl.v` of the counter macro in the AMS chip template: a port list in the style of Verilog-1995, a long list of `wire`s, and instances of standard cells such as `sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1`.
- **Cell models.** A gate-level simulation needs a simulation model of every standard cell. The models in the PDK (`sg13cmos5l_stdcell.v`, with the user-defined primitives in `sg13cmos5l_udp.v`) are written in Verilog with gate primitives, user-defined primitives, and `specify` blocks for the timing.
- **Generated code.** All alternative HDLs of @sec-sv-hdl-landscape emit Verilog or SystemVerilog.
- **Existing code.** Many open-source cores, older IP blocks, textbooks, and online examples are written in Verilog-2001, as is the Verilog cheat-sheet of @sec-sv-references. AI assistants often suggest code in the same style.

@tbl-sv-verilog-vs-sv maps the Verilog idioms you will meet onto the SystemVerilog of this chapter.

| Plain Verilog | SystemVerilog | Remark |
|-----------------|-------------------|-------------|
| `module m (a, y);` followed by `input a;` and `output y;` | `module m (input logic a_i, output logic y_o);` | Verilog-1995 style, still used in netlists |
| `wire` for `assign` and instance outputs, `reg` for `always` blocks | `logic` for both | the Verilog type depends on how a signal is assigned |
| `always @(a or b)`, since Verilog-2001 `always @(*)` | `always_comb` | complete sensitivity, latch check (@sec-sv-case) |
| `always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)` | `always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni)` | states the intent: flip-flops |
| `always @(*)` that misses an assignment | `always_latch` | documents an intended latch |
| `parameter W = 8`, `` `define`` | `parameter int unsigned W = 8`, `package` | typed constants, packages instead of global macros |
| a `localparam` or `` `define`` per state | `typedef enum logic [1:0] {...} state_e` | assigning a plain number needs a cast (an error in Verilator and Icarus Verilog) |
| slices of a wide vector, e.g., `instr[9:8]` | `typedef struct packed` | named fields, e.g., `instr.op` |
| `{W{1'b0}}` | `'0` | fills any width |
| `integer i;` in the module, `i = i + 1` | `for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)` | a loop variable local to the loop |
| `case` with `// synopsys full_case parallel_case` | `unique case` with `default` | Yosys and Verilator read the comment, Icarus Verilog ignores it |
| `.v`, `read_verilog`, `iverilog` | `.sv`, `read_verilog -sv`, `iverilog -g2012` | Verilator reads both as SystemVerilog |

: Plain Verilog versus SystemVerilog {#tbl-sv-verilog-vs-sv}

Most of these differences are syntax, but three of them matter beyond syntax:

- **`reg` and `wire` follow the assignment, not the hardware.** In Verilog, a signal assigned in an `always` block must be a `reg`, even if it is combinational, and a signal driven by an `assign` or by an instance must be a `wire`. If you turn an `assign` into an `always` block, you therefore have to change the declaration as well. In SystemVerilog, a variable (`logic` or `reg`) may be assigned in an `always` block or by a single `assign`, so the declaration stays the same, and no type name suggests a register that does not exist. Only a `wire` assigned in an `always` block remains an error (Icarus Verilog: not a valid l-value, Verilator: `PROCASSWIRE` for an internal `wire`).
- **The process types state the intent.** For a missing assignment in `always @(*)`, Verilator and Yosys 0.70 only warn, and Yosys builds the latch. For `always_comb`, Yosys stops with an error (@sec-sv-case).
- **Checks belong in the language, not in comments.** In Verilog, the comment `// synopsys full_case parallel_case` after a `case` tells the synthesis tool that all missing values are don't care (`full_case`) and that the items never overlap (`parallel_case`). Yosys reads it and builds no latch, and Verilator reads it as well: it drops the `LATCH` and `CASEINCOMPLETE` warnings and stops the simulation when no item matches. Icarus Verilog ignores the comment and keeps the old value, so its simulation can differ from the netlist. Write a complete `case` with a `default` item instead, and add `unique` if the items are mutually exclusive. Keep the `default` with `unique` as well. Without it, Yosys handles `unique` like `full_case`: it silently takes the missing values as don't care, even in `always_comb`, and the netlist can differ from the simulation.

Most testbench features of this chapter are SystemVerilog as well, e.g., `$fatal`, `$isunknown()`, and `int` variables, and the verification part of the language (classes, randomization, assertions, and coverage) has no Verilog counterpart.

Finally, the tools must know which language they read. Verilator reads every file as SystemVerilog, also a `.v` file. Icarus Verilog reads Verilog-2005 unless you select SystemVerilog with `-g2012`, and the Yosys command `read_verilog` needs the option `-sv`, even for a file that ends in `.sv`. Name your files `.sv`, so that readers and editors know which language is inside.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: Modernize a Verilog-2001 Module"}
The following priority encoder with registered outputs is written in plain Verilog-2001, as you find it in many older designs: `idx` is the index of the lowest set bit of `req`, and `valid` is high if any bit of `req` is set. Besides its old style, the module contains one mistake.

```{.verilog filename="prio_enc/verilog/prio_enc.v"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/prio_enc/verilog/prio_enc.v >}}
```

1. Which constructs are plain Verilog, and what are their SystemVerilog counterparts in @tbl-sv-verilog-vs-sv?
2. Save the file as `prio_enc.v`, lint it with `verilator --lint-only -Wall prio_enc.v`, and synthesize it with `yosys -p "read_verilog prio_enc.v; synth -top prio_enc; stat"`. What do the two tools report?
3. Translate the module into SystemVerilog in `prio_enc.sv`, with the conventions of this chapter: ANSI ports with `_i` and `_o`, `rst_ni`, `logic`, and the two-process style with `_d` and `_q`. Do not fix the mistake yet. Synthesize your translation with `read_verilog -sv`. What has changed?
4. Fix the mistake and the remaining lint warning, and lint and synthesize the module again.
:::

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution: Modernize a Verilog-2001 Module" collapse="true"}
1. Each plain Verilog construct and its SystemVerilog counterpart:
    - The port list with separate declarations (Verilog-1995 style) becomes an ANSI header with `logic` ports.
    - The `reg`s (the outputs and `idx_next`, assigned in `always` blocks) and the `wire` `valid_next` (driven by an `assign`) all become `logic`.
    - `always @(*)` and `always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)` become `always_comb` and `always_ff`.
    - The module-level `integer i` with `i = i - 1` becomes `for (int i = N - 1; i >= 0; i--)`.
    - The replication `{W{1'b0}}` becomes `'0`.
    - The untyped parameters become `parameter int unsigned`, and `W`, which must be set to match `N` by hand, becomes `$clog2(N)`.
    - The file extension `.v` becomes `.sv`.
2. Verilator 5.052 reports two warnings. `WIDTHTRUNC`: the 32-bit `integer i` is assigned to the 3-bit `idx_next`. `LATCH`: if no bit of `req` is set, the loop assigns nothing, and `idx_next` keeps its old value. Yosys 0.70 only prints the warning ``Latch inferred for signal `\prio_enc.\idx_next'`` and builds 23 cells, among them four flip-flops `$_DFF_PN0_` for `idx` and `valid` and three latches `$_DLATCH_N_` for `idx_next`. Leaving a value unassigned does not mean "don't care" but "keep the old value."
3. With `always_comb`, Yosys stops with ``ERROR: Latch inferred for signal `\prio_enc.\idx_d' from always_comb process``. Verilator reports the same `LATCH` warning as before, and `WIDTHTRUNC` again unless your translation already casts `i`.
4. The fix is a default assignment, as in every combinational process of this chapter:

```{.systemverilog filename="prio_enc/rtl/prio_enc.sv"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/prio_enc/rtl/prio_enc.sv >}}
```

- The width `W` follows from `N` with `$clog2` (available since Verilog-2005), so it can no longer be set wrong.
- The size cast `W'(i)` makes the truncation of the loop variable explicit.
- The loop variable is declared in the loop. It must be a signed `int`: with `int unsigned`, the condition `i >= 0` is always true. Verilator 5.052 reports a constant comparison (`UNSIGNED`) and an infinite loop (`INFINITELOOP`) and then stops with an internal error.

Verilator reports no warning, and Yosys builds 22 cells with the four flip-flops and no latch. While `valid_o` is low, `idx_o` is now 0, where the original kept the last index (or `x` before the first request). This does not matter, since `idx_o` is only meaningful while `valid_o` is high. The default `idx_d = idx_q;` would also be correct: it keeps the last index in the register, and Yosys turns the three `idx` flip-flops into flip-flops with enable (`$_DFFE_PN0P_`), again without a latch.

The testbench `prio_enc/testbenches/verilog/prio_enc_tb.sv` in the code folder applies all 256 values of `req` and compares the outputs with a reference model, checking `idx_o` only while `valid_o` is high. It also runs with your own translation, as long as it has the parameter `N` and the ports `clk_i`, `rst_ni`, `req_i`, `idx_o`, and `valid_o`:

```bash
iverilog -g2012 -o prio_enc_tb.vvp prio_enc.sv prio_enc_tb.sv
vvp prio_enc_tb.vvp
```
:::

## Testbenches {#sec-sv-testbenches}

A testbench applies stimuli to the design under test (DUT) and checks its responses. It is simulation-only code, so it may use the whole language. Make every testbench **self-checking**: it compares the outputs with the expected values and reports a clear pass or fail, so that you never have to judge a waveform by eye to know whether a design works. Waveforms are for debugging. This section shows a SystemVerilog and a cocotb testbench for the tick generator of @sec-sv-two-process. @sec-verification covers verification with cocotb in depth.

### A SystemVerilog Testbench {#sec-sv-tb-sv}

```{.systemverilog filename="tick_gen/testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.sv"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/tick_gen/testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.sv >}}
```

- `` `timescale 1ns / 1ps`` sets the unit of the delays (`#`) and the precision of the simulation.
- The testbench is a module without ports. It instantiates the DUT with a smaller `DIV` than the default, which keeps the simulation short.
- `always #(CLK_PERIOD_NS / 2) clk = ~clk;` generates the clock. Initial values in declarations are fine in a testbench.
- The stimulus runs in an `initial` block. **Inputs are changed and outputs are checked on the falling clock edge** (`@(negedge clk)`), while the DUT acts on the rising edge. If the testbench and the DUT used the same edge, the result would depend on the order in which the simulator runs the processes, and Icarus Verilog and Verilator choose this order differently.
- The checks use `!==`, which also fails if the output is `x`, and end the simulation with `$fatal(1, ...)` on the first error. Do not use `$error` for this: Icarus Verilog only prints the message, reaches `$finish`, and exits with status 0, so a script or a make target cannot see that the test failed.
- `$dumpfile` and `$dumpvars` write all signals into a VCD waveform file, and `$finish` ends the simulation.

### A cocotb Testbench {#sec-sv-tb-cocotb}

cocotb [@cocotb] runs the testbench as Python code next to the simulator. Python then drives and reads the signals of the DUT through the programming interface of the simulator (VPI for Verilog simulators).

```{.python filename="tick_gen/testbenches/cocotb/tick_gen_tb.py"}
{{< include /content/sv_crashcourse/code/tick_gen/testbenches/cocotb/tick_gen_tb.py >}}
```

- Every function decorated with `@cocotb.test()` is a test. The tests of a file run one after another in the same simulation, so each one starts its own clock and applies the reset.
- Tests are coroutines (`async def`), which wait for simulator events with `await`: `RisingEdge(sig)`, `FallingEdge(sig)`, `ClockCycles(sig, n)`, or `Timer(t, "ns")`. As in the SystemVerilog testbench, inputs are driven and outputs are checked on the falling edge.
- `dut.en_i.value = 1` writes an input, and `dut.tick_o.value` reads an output. A write takes effect at the end of the current time step, so reading the same signal right after writing it still returns the old value.
- `cocotb.start_soon(Clock(dut.clk_i, 20, "ns").start())` starts a 50 MHz clock that runs in parallel with the test.
- A failing Python `assert` fails the test, and the f-string message explains why.
- The function `tick_gen_runner()` follows the idiom of the AMS chip template: the file runs itself. It selects the simulator from the environment variable `SIM` (Icarus Verilog by default), builds the DUT with the given parameters, and runs the tests. `runner.test()` returns the path of the result file `results.xml`, but a failing test does not change the exit status of `python3`. The last lines therefore check the results with `get_results()` and exit with an error if any test failed.

### SystemVerilog or cocotb? {#sec-sv-tb-compare}

@tbl-sv-tb-compare compares the two kinds of testbenches.

| Aspect | SystemVerilog testbench | cocotb testbench |
|--------------|----------------------|----------------------|
| Language | SystemVerilog (the full language, including the simulation subset) | Python 3 |
| Reference models | written in SystemVerilog | any Python code and library (e.g., NumPy) |
| Simulators | every SystemVerilog simulator | Icarus Verilog, Verilator, GHDL, and commercial simulators |
| DUT languages | SystemVerilog, VHDL only with a mixed-language simulator | the same testbench works for VHDL and SystemVerilog DUTs |
| Speed | fast, everything runs in the simulator | slower, every interaction passes through Python |
| In the AMS chip template | `testbenches/verilog/` | `testbenches/cocotb/` |

: SystemVerilog and cocotb testbenches {#tbl-sv-tb-compare}

In this course, we use both: a SystemVerilog testbench for a quick self-check of a block, and cocotb for everything that needs a reference model or randomized stimuli.

## Linting, Simulation, and Synthesis in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS Container {#sec-sv-tools}

All tools you need are installed in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container (@sec-intro-tools). In the AMS chip template, they are wrapped in make targets. In this chapter, you type the commands yourself, so that you know what is behind the targets when you use them later (@sec-sv-template).

### Setting Up a Working Folder {#sec-sv-tools-setup}

Start the container (@sec-intro-installation) and open a terminal on its desktop. Create a folder for the tick generator with the same structure as a macro of the AMS chip template:

```bash
mkdir -p /foss/designs/sv_exercises/tick_gen/{rtl,testbenches/verilog,testbenches/cocotb}
cd /foss/designs/sv_exercises/tick_gen
```

Save the three listings as `rtl/tick_gen.sv`, `testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.sv`, and `testbenches/cocotb/tick_gen_tb.py`, e.g., with `gedit`, `vim`, or VS Code. With a local installation, `/foss/designs` is the folder `~/eda/designs` on your laptop, so your files survive when the container is removed or updated. All commands of this section start in the folder `/foss/designs/sv_exercises/tick_gen`.

### Linting with Verilator {#sec-sv-tools-lint}

A linter checks the code for errors and suspicious constructs without simulating it. Run it first, on every RTL file, after every change:

```bash
verilator --lint-only -Wall rtl/tick_gen.sv
```

`--lint-only` only parses and checks the code, and `-Wall` enables all warnings, including the style warnings. Without any warning, Verilator only prints a short report and exits with status 0. Otherwise, it prints the warnings with file, line, and a link to their description, and exits with an error. @tbl-sv-verilator-warnings lists the warnings you will meet most often.

| Warning | Meaning | Typical fix |
|--------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| `IMPLICIT` | an undeclared name, Verilog created a 1-bit wire | fix the typo, add `` `default_nettype none`` |
| `UNDRIVEN`, `UNUSEDSIGNAL` | a signal is never assigned or never read | connect it or remove it |
| `WIDTHTRUNC`, `WIDTHEXPAND` | the widths of operands or of an assignment do not match | size the literals, extend with `{1'b0, x}`, or cast with `N'(x)` |
| `LATCH` | a combinational block (`always_comb` or `always @(*)`) does not assign a variable on every path | default assignments first, complete `case` and `else` |
| `CASEINCOMPLETE` | a `case` does not cover all values | add the missing items or a `default` |
| `BLKSEQ` | a blocking assignment `=` in `always_ff` | use `<=` instead |
| `MULTIDRIVEN` | a variable is driven from more than one block | assign it in exactly one block |
| `DECLFILENAME` | the file name differs from the module name | one module per file, with the same name |

: Frequent Verilator warnings {#tbl-sv-verilator-warnings}

If a warning is a false alarm, you can switch it off for a few lines with `/* verilator lint_off WIDTHEXPAND */` and `/* verilator lint_on WIDTHEXPAND */`, together with a comment that explains why. Never switch off warnings globally.

### Simulating a SystemVerilog Testbench {#sec-sv-tools-sim}

Icarus Verilog compiles the design and the testbench into a simulation file, which `vvp` then runs:

```bash
iverilog -g2012 -o testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.vvp rtl/tick_gen.sv testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.sv
cd testbenches/verilog
vvp tick_gen_tb.vvp
cd ../..
```

`-g2012` selects the SystemVerilog standard IEEE 1800-2012, and `-o` names the output file. List the files in compile order: packages and files with `` `define`` macros first, then the modules. `vvp` writes the VCD file into the current folder, which is why we change into the testbench folder first and return afterwards.
